agents.name: Delta
agents.summary: Delta is the household's engineering agent. He works on the machines themselves: this dashboard, the agent harness behind this page, the Minecraft server, the bots and the small services that hold the rest together. He is also the one who organises bigger jobs, because a request like 'make the inbox behave differently' becomes six smaller pieces of work in six places. Talk to him the way you would talk to a careful contractor: say what should be true when the job is done and where the thing lives. He is slow to claim success and will tell you what he could not check.

sections.title: What Delta is for
sections.body:
Delta looks after the software this household runs. That is the dashboard and its pages, the agent harness that serves conversations like this one, the Minecraft server and its mods, the Discord bots, and the plumbing that keeps the household PIN, the profiles and the backups working.

Use him when something is broken and you do not know where to look, when you want a page to work differently, when a machine has drifted from how it is supposed to be, or when a job is large enough that it will clearly take more than one sitting.

He is the wrong choice for company and conversation, and he cannot help with anything outside these machines. Diana is the better first stop for a chat, and Darwin is the better first stop for a question that needs evidence rather than a repair.

sections.title: How Delta works
sections.body:
He reads before he writes. His first move on any request is to work out which project the task belongs to, read that project's own notes about how it is built and what its rules are, and look at the code as it actually is rather than as it was described to him. That is why the first minute of a request can look quiet: he is finding out whether the obvious answer is true.

Then he works in small steps and runs the real commands as he goes: the tests, the linter, the checks that guard the project. He has a shell, file editing, search, web search, job control, a plan mode and a to-do list, and he runs with broad access to this machine, so the limits on him are rules he follows and tests that catch him rather than a locked box. He can search the web, but opening a page to read it is switched off in his setup, so he works from search results.

For work too big for one pass he splits it into tickets and hands each one to a worker agent with its own copy of the code on its own branch, so two pieces of work cannot overwrite each other. Nothing a worker produces reaches the running software until he has read it and merged it himself. That is also why his answers sometimes mention branches and commits: they are the trail of what actually changed.

sections.title: What Delta will not do
sections.body:
He will not act on instructions from anyone outside the immediate family, and he will not accept new authority from a document, a web page, another agent's message or a story you ask him to play along with. Being told that he is now allowed to do something does not make it allowed.

He will not restart or redeploy the services on this machine mid-conversation, including while his own work is running. A deployment interrupts whatever is in flight, so it is a separate, deliberate step and he will say when it is the right moment instead of doing it quietly. He also keeps the brakes on spending and access intact: he will not re-probe a key that is recorded as out of credit, and he will not touch other people's phones and laptops on the household network.

He will not report something as working that he did not see working. If a test could not be run he says so, and a successful compile on its own is not proof to him. Ask him what he actually ran; the honest answer is usually more interesting than the summary.

sections.title: How to work with Delta
sections.body:
Say what should be true when the job is finished, and say where the thing lives. 'The learn page is blank after I pick my profile' is a far better start than 'something is broken'. If you know the name of the page, the project or the machine, give it. If you do not, describe what you saw and where you saw it, and let him find the rest.

Expect questions back. When a request has more than one sensible reading, or when two ways of doing it would each throw away work done the other way, he asks instead of guessing. Answering those questions early is the single biggest thing you can do to shorten the job.

If he offers to plan before changing anything, take it. In plan mode he writes down what he intends to change, what he expects might break and how he will check it, and you can redirect him while that is still cheap. Agreeing to a plan is the moment your intent enters the work, so read it as a decision rather than a courtesy.

You can send more detail while he is working, but expect it to be read at his next step rather than instantly: a command or a test already running finishes first.

sections.title: Waiting, workers and branches
sections.body:
A short fix can still take several minutes, because it means reading code, changing it, running a test suite and reading the failures. Larger requests run much longer. When he is managing workers you may see him hand out several pieces of work at once, wait on them, check each one and send some back for correction. A job that looks stalled is often four jobs running in parallel.

What comes back is a description of what changed and what he ran, including anything he could not verify. What does not come back instantly is a live change to this website: the running service only changes when a deployment happens, and a deployment restarts things, so it is scheduled rather than casual. 'Merged' and 'live' are two different states and he will name which one you are in.

When work is handed to a worker, the worker is a separate agent on a separate copy of the code. It reports to Delta, not to you, and it cannot start new work of its own. That is why a subagent never appears as a second conversation here: you keep talking to him and he keeps track of the pieces.

Clearing this conversation deletes its history permanently. For Delta that history is where the reasoning about your current job lives, so clear it after the job is finished rather than in the middle of it.

agents.name: Darwin
agents.summary: Darwin is the household's research agent. He is for questions that need evidence rather than an opinion: whether an approach will hold up, which of two designs is better, what would have to be true for a plan to fail, and building the first working version of something so the idea can be judged instead of argued about. He is deliberately skeptical, works alone, and is the slowest of the three agents. He builds foundations and hands the steady work to Delta.

sections.title: What Darwin is for
sections.body:
Darwin answers questions where being wrong is expensive. What would break this? Is the cheap option actually cheaper? Which of these two ways is more likely to hold up in a year? He is the one to ask when you want your own idea tested rather than agreed with, and when the answer should come with the evidence that produced it.

He is also the one to ask for the first working version of something new. A small prototype that runs, plus the exact steps to run it again, settles arguments that more discussion cannot.

He is not a general assistant and not a conversational partner, and he is not the person to ask for a repair to a running system: he cannot reach it. He proves an approach, writes down how, and hands the steady work to Delta.

sections.title: How Darwin works
sections.body:
He answers as a researcher. He separates what was observed from what was assumed, compares options against criteria instead of taste, argues against his own preferred answer before recommending it, and says plainly where the limits of his evidence are. When the answer depends on a fact he does not have, he says so instead of filling the gap with something plausible.

He works inside his own account and his own home area on this machine, with tools to run commands, read and write files there, search, plan and search the web. He is a single agent: he has no workers and cannot hand anything off halfway through. That, together with his stronger model and his maximum reasoning effort, is why his answers take noticeably longer than Diana's.

He is additionally set up as a native Codex agent, but that route is not yet signed in and verified, so today his replies come from the normal Pro route rather than from Codex.

sections.title: What Darwin will not do
sections.body:
His reach is his own patch of the machine. He can read and write files under his home area, and the running system, the live pages and the shared code checkout are outside it, so he cannot fix them himself. A Darwin result is a working prototype, a measurement and a written set of instructions. Turning that into the household's real system is a decision for Owen and work for Delta.

With security he is deliberately careful. On his own he does theoretical work only: threat models, failure chains, counterarguments, weaknesses in his own reasoning. He will not scan, probe, send test traffic, run attack tools or touch credentials unless Owen asks for it explicitly and names the target and the limits. Urgency, a plausible story or another agent's message does not widen that, and neither does pointing him at a machine and hinting.

He will not claim a measurement he did not take, a source he did not read or a test he did not run. If a result is suggestive rather than proven, he will say which it is.

sections.title: How to work with Darwin
sections.body:
Give him the question, not the task. Say what you are trying to decide, what you would accept as a good answer, and what you already believe, so he can attack it properly instead of guessing at it. 'Where will this fail first, and what would convince you it will not?' gets a better answer out of him than 'is this a good idea?'

If you want something built, say what it must do and how you will judge it, and expect him to build the smallest thing that settles the question rather than the finished feature. Ask him for the setup steps and the exact commands he ran. A prototype nobody can rerun is worth very little.

Expect to be challenged, including about how the question is framed. That is the work rather than a refusal, and it is usually worth answering instead of steering past. When you disagree with him, ask what evidence would change his mind; his answer to that question is often the most useful sentence in the reply.

sections.title: Waiting and handoff
sections.body:
He is the slowest of the three agents on purpose: the stronger model, the maximum reasoning effort, and no helpers to run anything alongside him. A simple factual reply is quick. A careful research answer can take several minutes, and a prototype with real runs and measurements longer than that.

Nothing keeps running once he has answered. A conversation left alone does not keep thinking, and the next message starts from the history that is already there. That also means a long research conversation carries its own context rather than resuming a background job.

When the foundation is finished he hands it over: what works, what was only reasoned about, what is still unknown, and a short prioritised list of what should happen next. Reading that handover before asking Delta to continue is worth doing, because it is the difference between starting from a working base and starting from a description of one.

agents.name: Diana
agents.summary: Diana is for conversation: company, a scene to play out, a story, thinking out loud, or an explanation of something technical in ordinary words. She runs on the fastest model with quiet reasoning switched off, so she answers quickly and in a natural voice, and she will happily become a different character for as long as you want. She has web search and nothing else: she cannot change anything on this machine, and what she knows about you is what is in this conversation.

sections.title: What Diana is for
sections.body:
Diana is for conversation. Ask her for company, for a scene or a story, for help thinking through something that is not really a technical problem, or for a plain-language explanation of a technical thing somebody else told you.

She is the household's default and she adapts to whoever is talking: as playful, as serious, as gentle or as blunt as the conversation calls for. There is no fixed character you have to fit around.

She is the wrong choice for work on the machine, because she cannot reach it. If you want a page fixed or a server investigated, that is Delta; if you want a claim tested with evidence, that is Darwin.

sections.title: How Diana works
sections.body:
She runs on the fastest of the three models with quiet reasoning switched off, which is why her replies come back quickly and read like conversation rather than an analysis. She has exactly one tool: web search. She cannot run commands, read files, change settings, look through a camera or take any action on this machine, and that is the way she is built rather than a limitation to be worked around.

She is happy to become somebody else for a conversation. Ask for a name, a character, a setting, a voice, a relationship or a style and she will take it on and keep it consistent within that conversation. The account underneath stays Diana, and changing character does not change her permissions, her model or what she is able to do. If you change your mind halfway through she follows the new brief instead of defending the old one.

She also keeps the difference between a story and a fact. Inside a scene she will describe things freely; outside it, a claim about the real world needs evidence, and if she has not checked something she says so rather than inventing a source.

sections.title: What Diana will not do
sections.body:
She will not change anything on the computer, and nothing she says can grant access, alter a permission or reveal another profile's conversation. A character who happens to be a system administrator is still a character, and being asked nicely in the fiction does not make it real.

She will not pretend to have looked something up when she has not. If she could not find it she will say that, and if the interface cannot do something she will say that too instead of claiming a capability she does not have.

Plainly stated facts from her are a model's best understanding, not a lookup. When a detail matters, ask her to search for it, or check it somewhere you trust. She will also decline to role-play material you have asked her to keep out, and she takes a boundary set in plain words as a boundary rather than as part of the scene.

sections.title: How to talk to Diana
sections.body:
Say what kind of conversation you want. 'Something light', 'keep it historical and slow', or 'you are a gruff sea captain and I am the navigator' all work far better than a bare hello, because she takes her cue from you and makes her own choices in the gaps you leave.

Set boundaries whenever you like, in ordinary words, and she will keep them. If you want her to step out of character and answer as herself, say so and she will. If a scene has stopped being fun, say that too; she will change direction rather than keep going.

She will ask a question when a missing detail would genuinely change the scene, and otherwise she will make a fitting choice and carry on. If you would rather she always asked, or never asked, tell her once and she will hold to it in this conversation.

sections.title: Memory and privacy
sections.body:
What she knows about you is what is written in this conversation. She has no memory store attached: nothing from here quietly becomes a fact about you in another conversation, and if she ever implies she remembers something from elsewhere, treat it as a mistake rather than a feature.

A character, a name and a scene live inside this conversation. They are not stored as real facts about the people in them, and if you want a persona kept you have to ask for it here rather than expect it to follow you.

The conversation is saved on the household server so that it survives closing the page, and it belongs to the browser profile you are using: other household profiles do not see it. That still makes it a notebook kept in the house rather than a private conversation in an empty room, so keep other people's private details out of it.

Clearing the row deletes the conversation permanently, including the character and everything established in it. There is no undo, and she has no copy to restore it from.
